summary:
Bitlis province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package would amend the national penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", criminalise participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to 4 years in prison, and raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a mandatory permanent-infertility condition. Health professionals who perform such care would face punishment under the draft. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 Turkish LGBT groups together with the Turkish Medical Association oppose it.

Kaos GL reported that its 2025 report, "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility becoming institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

Street-level enforcement illustrates how this operates. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

That document obligation is general: Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Each province in Türkiye faces the same national regime; the enforcement pattern is illustrated most clearly in Istanbul, where 2025 street stops and GBT checks were documented, and the sub-national data points of Ankara (Sincan Women's Prison) and Kayseri (Provincial Health Directorate circular) show the policy reaching detention and health administration. None of those units represents a separate legal regime, and no reporting in this inventory describes a distinct Bitlis practice.

The depth of the pattern predates current policy. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025, with the Poyraz case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and coordinated demands for an independent investigation from Human Rights Association branches across six cities. Contestation has not yet produced a change in placement rules, which remain based on registered sex.

The draft 11th Judicial Package has drawn coordinated institutional opposition: 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object to the care-age increase and infertility mandate. The status of the package after October 2025 is not established in this inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bitlis live under the same national penal, civil and health frameworks described for visitors, and the draft 11th Judicial Package would extend criminal liability to residents for conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, with up to 4 years for participating in same-sex ceremonies.

Gender-affirming care for residents would be restricted by the draft to those aged 25 and over with mandatory permanent infertility, with health professionals exposed to punishment and 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposing the measure. The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular already affect how medical-board reports are issued, barring the "other" option and requiring e-reports.

Trans people in custody are placed by registered sex, and LGBT detainees face arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, restricted healthcare, disrupted visits, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can invite further violence, according to the Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data.

Domestic advocacy and documentation continue: Kaos GL published its 2025 report through lawyer Kerem Dikmen, and Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated demands for an independent inquiry into the death of the trans prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bitlis-specific incident, enforcement action, LGBT organisation, pride event or provincial health directive appears in the source inventory; the province's profile is derived entirely from national reporting and from documented practice in other provinces, and local conditions remain unresolved on that basis.

The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved beyond Human Rights Watch's report of 29 October 2025; whether it has been tabled, amended or enacted is not sourced here.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular have been implemented through a Bitlis health authority is not sourced. Nor is any figure for detentions, stops or documented violations in Bitlis for 2025 or 2024.

The legal analysis of GBT checks as a possible violation of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in the reporting and has not been tested by a court in the material available; no ruling on the practice is documented here.
